---
title: "Can a correlation statistic miss a strong nonlinear relationship?"
---

## What the question asks

Can a correlation statistic miss a strong nonlinear relationship?

## Steps to decide and solve

Calculate Pearson correlation but do not stop there; make a scatterplot; inspect curved and clustered patterns, leverage points, and the data range.

## Worked example: anscombe

```{r}
#| eval: false
d <- ru_data("anscombe")
# Anscombe's real x2 values; the square is a NEW, constructed response.
constructed <- data.frame(deviation=d$x2-mean(d$x2))
constructed$squared <- constructed$deviation^2
r <- ru_apply("zero_correlation", data=constructed,
              x="deviation", y="squared")
stopifnot(abs(r)<1e-10)
# Compare with one of the original Anscombe pairs:
ru_apply("zero_correlation", data=d, x="x2", y="y2")
```

The deliberately constructed quadratic relationship has zero Pearson correlation by symmetry, despite a perfect curved relationship. Anscombe's observed example also demonstrates why similarly sized correlations cannot replace inspection of a plot. Only the x2 values in the constructed example come from the dataset; the squared response is not a recorded measurement.

## Apply it to another question

```r
ru_apply("zero_correlation", data=your_data, x="first_numeric_column", y="second_numeric_column")
```

If the question concerns monotonic ranks, explore Spearman correlation. Neither Pearson nor Spearman covers every possible dependence pattern.

Use `ru_plan("zero_correlation")` to inspect alternative routes when required information is absent or uncertain.
